title: Privilege mapping and permission matrices for resource-scoped RBAC v2
creator: Maya Chen
description: Design a role model and permission-mapping approach for RBAC v2 that supports hierarchical resources, scoped grants (prefix, exact, wildcard), admin delegation, and contextual audit linkage. This ticket produces the canonical permission matrix, decisions on inheritance semantics, audit log scoping rules, and SSO/SAML attribute mapping guidance for provisioning and attribute-based role bindings.
acceptance_criteria: A canonical permissions matrix exists as CSV and is reviewed by Security, Platform, and Product
Inheritance semantics documented (override vs additive) with examples for Org > Tenant > Project resources
Audit log fields and correlation keys defined so actions can be filtered by role, scope, and request context
SSO/SAML mapping doc with recommended attributes for group-to-role sync and just-in-time role assertions
Implementation checklist for runtime enforcement and migration plan for existing role bindings
design_decisions: Scope representation: use path-like scope identifiers (e.g., org/:id/tenant/:id/project/:id) to enable prefix matching and least-privilege grants
Inheritance model: additive-by-default with explicit deny not supported in v1; admin-level grants can declare 'sealed' scopes to prevent inheritance where necessary
Role vs Permission: roles are named groupings of fine-grained permissions (read/write/admin/impersonate) to allow easy mapping to SSO groups and UI checkboxes
Audit correlation: include role, effective_scope, principal_id, session_id, and sso_assertion_id in each audit entry to enable filtered investigations and compliance reports
open_questions: Should we support explicit deny rules in RBAC v2 or wait for v3 after rollout? Pros: clearer conflict resolution. Cons: increased enforcement complexity.
How to model cross-tenant read-only federation for platform teams without giving admin surface?
What minimal SAML attributes should be required for provisioning vs optional for enrichment (e.g., 'roles' vs 'groups' vs custom 'redwood_scope')?
implementation_notes: Enforcement will be layered: authorization middleware verifies token -> resolves role bindings -> expands effective scopes -> checks permission set for route
Cache effective role bindings per principal with TTL tied to SSO session expiry and explicit invalidation hooks on role binding change
Migration: provide a compatibility shim that maps existing role sets to new scoped roles, log all mapped decisions for one-cycle audit review before enforcement
Audit log writing: emit structured JSON record with fields listed in design_decisions and include 'allowed_by' referencing role_key and binding_id

decision_rationale: We chose a path-like scoping model because it maps directly to our resource graph, simplifies prefix-based grants, and is compatible with existing route patterns. Additive inheritance reduces surprise for users during rollout and minimizes accidental privilege revocation. Strong audit correlation fields are required to meet compliance needs and to support forensic timelines across SSO assertions and runtime sessions.
migration_plan: 1) Generate mapping report from current role bindings to scoped roles and surface to tenants for review
2) Run opt-in enforcement mode that logs mismatches for 2 weeks
3) Notify customers with high-risk bindings and offer assistance
4) Flip enforcement flag at org-level with rollback window and audit review
